title: A finite-type monomorphism containing an entire nilpotent tower is an isomorphism
statement: Use schemes [def-pc-scheme], affine spectra [def-weil-affine-spectrum], and locally finite type morphisms [def-weil-finite-type-morphism], in the universes of [def-weil-size-convention]. Let $(A_n)_{n\geq1}$ be an inverse sequence of commutative rings with surjective transition maps whose kernels consist of nilpotent elements, and put $A=\varprojlim_n A_n$. Let $T$ be a scheme and let $h:T\to\operatorname{Spec}A$ be a monomorphism, meaning that for every scheme $B$ the map $\operatorname{Hom}(B,T)\to\operatorname{Hom}(B,\operatorname{Spec}A)$ is injective. Assume $h$ is locally of finite type. If for every $n\geq1$ the canonical map $\operatorname{Spec}A_n\to\operatorname{Spec}A$ factors through $h$, Then $h$ is an isomorphism.

proof.text: Put $S=\operatorname{Spec}A$, $S_n=\operatorname{Spec}A_n$, and write $i_n:S_n\to S$ for the canonical maps. Choose factorizations $a_n:S_n\to T$ with $h a_n=i_n$. They are unique since $h$ is a monomorphism. For each transition $r_n:S_n\to S_{n+1}$, the equality $h a_{n+1}r_n=i_n=h a_n$ gives $a_{n+1}r_n=a_n$. Here the direction of $r_n$ is opposite to that of $A_{n+1}\twoheadrightarrow A_n$.

Write $\pi_n:A\to A_n$ for the projections. Each $\pi_n$ is surjective: lift an element successively to $A_{n+1},A_{n+2},\ldots$ and use its images for the earlier coordinates. We also need that every $u\in A$ with $\pi_1(u)=1$ is a unit. Inductively $u_n=\pi_n(u)$ is a unit: given $u_n^{-1}$, lift it to $v\in A_{n+1}$; then $u_{n+1}v=1+e$ for a nilpotent element $e$ of the transition kernel. If $e^N=0$, multiplication by $\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}(-e)^j$ corrects $v$ to an inverse of $u_{n+1}$. The inverses $u_n^{-1}$ are compatible because a ring map preserves inverses and inverses are unique. Thus $(u_n^{-1})_n\in A$ is the inverse of $u$. This uses elementwise nilpotence only, not a uniform nilpotence exponent.

source.place: Tag 0CTJ, last paragraph; More on Algebra Tag 0CT7 (lemma-limit-henselian), first proof paragraph, with its unit argument written out

proof.text: Every open subset $U\subseteq S$ containing $i_1(S_1)$ equals $S$. Indeed write $U=\bigcup_\lambda D(f_\lambda)$ in the Zariski topology. Pullback to $S_1$ gives a cover by $D(\pi_1(f_\lambda))$, since a prime contains $f_\lambda$ in its inverse image exactly when it contains $\pi_1(f_\lambda)$. By the unit-ideal criterion in the cited node there are finitely many coefficients $b_j\in A_1$ with $\sum_j b_j\pi_1(f_j)=1$. Lift the coefficients using Step 2 and put $c=\sum_j\widetilde b_j f_j$. Then $\pi_1(c)=1$, so $c$ is a unit by Step 2. A prime containing all the $f_j$ contains $c$; consequently $S=D(c)\subseteq\bigcup_jD(f_j)\subseteq U$. This proves the required assertion about opens without invoking the stronger henselian-pair conclusion.

source.place: Tag 0CTJ, final assertion about opens; Tag 0CT7, first proof paragraph; Algebra Tag 00E0 (lemma-Zariski-topology), unit-ideal criterion

proof.text: For each transition, surjectivity gives the positive-power condition with exponent $1$, and its kernel consists of nilpotents. Thus the spectrum homeomorphism node applies to $A_{n+1}\to A_n$: every $r_n$ is surjective on points. Step 1 now gives $a_n(S_n)=a_{n+1}(S_{n+1})$ for all $n$. Their common image $K=a_1(S_1)$ is quasi-compact: an open cover pulls back along the continuous map $a_1$ to an open cover of the quasi-compact affine scheme $S_1$, hence has a finite subcover on $K$. Cover $K$ by affine opens of $T$ using the affine-basis node and choose a finite subcover. Let $T'$ be their union and $k:T'\hookrightarrow T$ its open immersion. Each chosen affine is quasi-compact by the affine qcqs node, so their finite union is quasi-compact. Since each $a_n$ has image in $T'$, restriction of its locally ringed-space map gives $a'_n:S_n\to T'$ with $k a'_n=a_n$; these maps remain compatible.

source.place: Tag 0CTJ, first proof paragraph; Algebra Tag 0BR8 (lemma-powers); Schemes Tag 01IT (lemma-basis-affine-opens)

proof.text: Let $q=h k:T'\to S$. It is a monomorphism, since $h$ and the open inclusion $k$ cancel morphisms. It is locally of finite type by the following explicit restriction argument. For each affine open $V=\operatorname{Spec}R$ in $S$, cover $h^{-1}(V)$ by $\operatorname{Spec}C$ with $C$ a finitely generated $R$-algebra. The basic-open-basis node covers $T'\cap\operatorname{Spec}C$ by $D(b)$ contained in that intersection. The principal-localization open-immersion node identifies each $D(b)$ with $\operatorname{Spec}C_b$. If $c_1,\ldots,c_r$ generate $C$ over $R$, the fraction description of localization shows that $c_1,\ldots,c_r,b^{-1}$ generate $C_b$ over $R$. This is the required affine cover for $q$. Apply the monomorphism-composite node with $f=q$ and $g=\mathrm{id}_S$; it says exactly that $q$ is separated and quasi-finite at every point. The affine qcqs node makes $S$ quasi-compact and quasi-separated. Since $T'$ is quasi-compact, clause (1) of the qcqs-permanence node makes $q$ quasi-compact. Together with local finite type this makes $q$ of finite type, by the cited definition. All hypotheses of the Zariski-main factorization node are now available.

source.place: Tag 0CTJ, second proof paragraph; Morphisms Tag 0CT8 (lemma-monomorphism-loc-finite-type-loc-quasi-finite)

proof.text: By Zariski main choose $T'\xrightarrow{j}W\xrightarrow{p}S$ with $j$ a quasi-compact open immersion, $p$ finite, and $p j=q$. A finite morphism is affine by the finite-morphism definition; since $S$ is affine, $W$ is affine. Write $W=\operatorname{Spec}B$. The maps $b_n=j a'_n:S_n\to W$ correspond to compatible ring homomorphisms $\beta_n:B\to A_n$, by the affine-spectrum correspondence. If $\alpha:A\to B$ corresponds to $p$, then $\beta_n\alpha=\pi_n$ for every $n$.

source.place: Tag 0CTJ, Zariski-main factorization and displayed ring diagram; More on Morphisms Tag 05K0 (lemma-quasi-finite-separated-pass-through-finite)

proof.text: The compatible homomorphisms $\beta_n$ define $\beta:B\to A$ explicitly by $\beta(b)=(\beta_n(b))_n$. Ring operations are coordinatewise, so this is a ring homomorphism. Its composite $\beta\alpha$ has all coordinates equal to those of the identity of $A$, hence is the identity. By affine-spectrum functoriality, $\beta$ gives $g:S\to W$ with $p g=\mathrm{id}_S$ and $g i_n=b_n=j a'_n$ for all $n$.

source.place: Tag 0CTJ, displayed ring diagram and the morphism from S to W

proof.text: Form $P=T'\times_{W,g}S$ with projections $e:P\to T'$ and $v:P\to S$. Base change of the open immersion $j$ makes $v$ an open immersion, so it identifies $P$ with an open subset $U\subseteq S$. The equality $j a'_1=g i_1$ from Step 7 gives a map $S_1\to P$ whose composite with $v$ is $i_1$, by the fibre-product universal property. Thus $i_1(S_1)\subseteq U$, and Step 3 yields $U=S$. The definition of open immersion therefore makes $v$ an isomorphism. Let $s'=e v^{-1}:S\to T'$. Since $j e=g v$ and $p j=q$, we have $q e=p g v=v$, whence $q s'=\mathrm{id}_S$.

source.place: Tag 0CTJ, final paragraph: open pullback containing the stage spectra

proof.text: Put $s=k s':S\to T$. Then $h s=q s'=\mathrm{id}_S$. Moreover $h(s h)=(h s)h=h=h\mathrm{id}_T$, so monicity of $h$ gives $s h=\mathrm{id}_T$. Thus $s$ is a two-sided inverse of $h$, proving the assertion for the original, possibly non-quasi-compact $T$.
